title: A missing theorem on dual spaces

candidates.exact_quote: Let T : X → Y be a continuous real linear map between complex Banach spaces, and let T_m be T regarded as a real linear map from Min_C(X) to Min_C(Y). Then ‖T_m‖_cb = ‖T‖.
candidates.claim_content: Definitions used by the paper: for a complex Banach space Z, Min_C(Z) is the minimal complex operator space structure on Z, whose matrix norms are given by ||[z_ij]||_{M_n(Min_C(Z))} = sup{ ||[psi(z_ij)]||_{M_n(C)} : psi a complex-linear functional on Z with ||psi|| <= 1 }. For a real-linear map T : X -> Y between complex Banach spaces, T_m denotes T viewed as a real-linear map Min_C(X) -> Min_C(Y), with amplifications (T_m)_n([x_ij]) = [T(x_ij)] and ||T_m||_cb = sup_n ||(T_m)_n||. CLAIM OF THE PAPER: ||T_m||_cb = ||T|| for every bounded real-linear T. PROPOSED COUNTEREXAMPLE: take X = C ⊕_1 C (two-dimensional complex ell^1, so ||(a,b)|| = |a|+|b|, with dual ball = {(lambda,mu) : |lambda| <= 1, |mu| <= 1}), Y = C (so Min_C(Y) = C with the usual M_n(C) norms), and T(a,b) = a + conj(b), which is real-linear with ||T|| = sup{|a + conj(b)| : |a|+|b| <= 1} = 1. Put P = (1/2)[[1,-i],[i,1]] and Q = (1/2)[[1,i],[-i,1]]: these are complementary orthogonal projections in M_2(C) (P+Q=I, PQ=0), and entrywise conjugation sends Q to P. Define [x_ij] in M_2(X) by x_ij = (P_ij, Q_ij). Then ||[x_ij]||_{M_2(Min_C(X))} = sup_{|lambda|,|mu| <= 1} ||lambda P + mu Q||_{M_2(C)} = 1, while [T(x_ij)] = P + conj(Q) = 2P has norm 2. Hence ||T_m||_cb >= 2 > 1 = ||T||.
candidates.suspected_defect: The proposition appears to be false for genuinely real-linear maps between complex spaces: the explicit 2x2 example gives cb norm at least 2 while the norm is 1. (The general decomposition T = T_1 + T_2 into complex-linear and conjugate-linear parts only gives ||T_m||_cb <= ||T_1|| + ||T_2|| <= 2||T||, and the two parts can attain their norms at different points, as in the example.)

candidates.error_location: Proof of Proposition 2.3, first sentence of the converse direction
candidates.exact_quote: Since φ ∘ T is a contractive real functional for all φ ∈ Ball(Y†), it is clear that T : Min_R(X) → Min_C(Y) is a complete contraction.
candidates.claim_content: Setting: X, Y complex Banach spaces, T : X -> Y a real-linear contraction. Min_R(Z) denotes the minimal REAL operator space structure on the underlying real space of Z, with matrix norms ||[z_ij]||_{M_n(Min_R(Z))} = sup{ ||[phi(z_ij)]||_{M_n(R)} : phi a real-linear functional on Z, ||phi|| <= 1 }; Min_C(Y) denotes the minimal COMPLEX operator space structure, with matrix norms sup over complex-linear contractive functionals psi of ||[psi(y_ij)]||_{M_n(C)}. The paper infers from the fact that phi∘T is a contractive real functional for each phi in Ball(Y†) that T : Min_R(X) -> Min_C(Y) is completely contractive.
candidates.suspected_defect: The displayed justification only controls the matrix norms computed with REAL functionals on Y, i.e. it shows T : Min_R(X) -> Min_R(Y) is completely contractive. But Min_R(Y) has strictly smaller matrix norms than Min_C(Y) viewed as a real operator space (e.g. for Y = C the matrix Z = [[1,-i],[i,1]] has ||Z||_{M_2(C)} = 2 while sup_theta ||Re(e^{i theta} Z)||_{M_2(R)} = 1, since cos(theta) I - sin(theta) J is orthogonal), as the paper itself notes in Example 2 / [35, Prop. 2.8]. So the inference goes in the wrong direction and does not establish complete contractivity into Min_C(Y).

candidates.error_location: Proof of Theorem 4.1, paragraph beginning 'We endow Y with its (complex) minimal operator space structure'
candidates.exact_quote: Then $Y$ is a complex operator space, and $q$ is a weak$^*$ continuous completely contractive real linear projection by Proposition 2.3.
candidates.claim_content: In the proof of Theorem 4.1 (if the real dual Y of a real Banach space X has isometric complex Banach space structure then X has isometric complex structure), the map q : Y^{**} -> Y is a weak*-continuous real-linear contractive projection obtained as the dual of the inclusion i_X : X -> Y^† transported through the identification Y^{**} ≅ Y^{††} of Lemma 1.3. Y is given its minimal COMPLEX operator space structure Min_C(Y), and Y^{**} its complex operator space bidual structure. The paper asserts that q is then COMPLETELY contractive, citing Proposition 2.3 ('for T real-linear between complex Banach spaces, T regarded as a map Min_C(X) -> Min_C(Y) satisfies ||T_m||_cb = ||T||'). The subsequent argument (Paulsen trick, extension to R : A^{**} -> A by injectivity of A = I(S(Y)), rigidity, multiplicative-domain theorem) requires q to be exactly completely contractive, not merely completely bounded.
candidates.suspected_defect: Proposition 2.3 appears to be false for real-linear maps (see the counterexample X = C ⊕_1 C, Y = C, T(a,b) = a + conj(b), which has norm 1 but cb norm >= 2 between the minimal complex operator space structures). If so, q is only known to be completely bounded with cb norm <= 2, and the unital complete contraction Q : S_R(Y^{**}) -> S_R(Y) produced by the Paulsen trick, and hence the whole argument of Theorem 4.1, is not justified. Note that q cannot be assumed complex-linear, since its complex linearity is essentially the conclusion being proved.

candidates.exact_quote: It is easy to see by duality theory that J² = I (since (J²)* = -I).
candidates.claim_content: Setting: X a real operator space whose real operator space dual X^† carries a complex operator space structure; Y denotes X^† with that complex structure; u = L_i is multiplication by i on Y, shown to be weak*-continuous; J : X -> X is the predual map of L_i, i.e. J^* = L_i. Since (J^2)^* = (J^*)^2 = (L_i)^2 = L_{i^2} = -I, one concludes J^2 = -I. The paper instead writes 'J^2 = I'. The criterion subsequently used (a map J on a real Banach space gives an isometric complex structure with ix = Jx iff J^2 = -I and x -> sx + tJ(x) is isometric whenever s^2+t^2=1) requires J^2 = -I, and the later remark that sI + tJ has inverse sI - tJ also requires J^2 = -I (since (sI+tJ)(sI-tJ) = s^2 I - t^2 J^2 = (s^2+t^2) I).
candidates.suspected_defect: Sign error: the parenthetical '(J^2)^* = -I' correctly yields J^2 = -I, not J^2 = I; as written the displayed conclusion contradicts both its own justification and the criterion for complex structure invoked immediately afterwards.

candidates.exact_quote: If M has complex Banach space structure then Lᵢ is a complex Banach space centralizer, and the latter commute with every M-projection (see e.g. [22, Section I.3]). In particular if the second summand is not (0) then Lᵢ commutes with (0, 1) ∈ M, which forces L∞(X, ℝ) to have complex Banach space structure.
candidates.claim_content: Setting: A is a real commutative C*-algebra whose real bidual M = A^{††} is real *-isomorphic to L^infty(Omega, C) ⊕_infty L^infty(X, R). Suppose M, as a REAL Banach space, carries an isometric complex structure, i.e. a real-linear map L_i : M -> M with L_i^2 = -I and s I + t L_i isometric whenever s^2 + t^2 = 1. The paper asserts that L_i is then a 'complex Banach space centralizer' of M and that, since centralizers commute with every M-projection, L_i commutes with the M-projection onto the summand L^infty(X, R), hence that summand inherits a complex structure. Note that in the paper's Closing Remark it is explicitly asserted that multiplication by i on a complex Banach space is NOT a real Banach space centralizer or multiplier: 'L_i ∉ Cent_R(X)'.
candidates.suspected_defect: The argument seems to contradict the paper's own Closing Remark: the M-projection onto L^infty(X,R) is a projection of M as a REAL Banach space, so commuting with it requires L_i to lie in the REAL centralizer Cent_R(M), which the Closing Remark says fails. Being a 'complex centralizer' of M with respect to the new complex structure only gives commutation with complex-linear M-projections, and the real M-projection onto the second summand is not a priori complex-linear. The step 'L_i commutes with (0,1)' therefore appears unjustified.

candidates.exact_quote: By uniqueness this is the isometry \( \mu \) in the proof, and we will need this fact later.
candidates.claim_content: In Lemma 1.3 one constructs a real-linear isometric weak*-homeomorphism mu : Y^{**} -> E^{††}, where Y is a complex Banach space and E = Y_r is its underlying real space (mu = ((j_Y)^†)^{-1} ∘ j_{Y^*}). In Remark 1 the paper considers rho : E^{††} -> Y^{**}, the unique weak*-continuous real-linear extension of the canonical map E -> Y -> Y^{**}, x -> i_Y(x), with i_E(x) mapping to i_Y(x), and asserts 'By uniqueness this is the isometry mu in the proof'. However mu maps Y^{**} to E^{††}, while rho maps E^{††} to Y^{**}; later, in the proof of Lemma 3.2, the paper correctly states 'By the Remark 1 after Lemma 1.3 we have that mu^{-1} is the unique weak* continuous real linear extension rho'.
candidates.suspected_defect: Direction mismatch: rho should be identified with mu^{-1}, not mu, as the paper itself states later in Lemma 3.2. Internal inconsistency in the identification of the maps.

candidates.error_location: Proof of Theorem 3.3 (3), conclusion after the displayed two-sided inequality
candidates.exact_quote: $$\|[x_{kl}]\|_{M_n(X)} \leq \|[x_{kl}]\|_{M_n(W)} \leq 2\|[x_{kl}]\|_{M_n(X)}$$ for all $n$ and $x_{kl} \in X$. Thus $W$ is a real isometric copy of $X$ but with an equivalent operator space renorming.
candidates.claim_content: Setting: X is a real operator space whose real operator space dual X^† carries a complex operator space structure, Y = X^† with that complex structure, W is X regarded as a complex Banach space (via the complex structure J obtained from L_i) and given the operator space structure making the canonical embedding i_W : W -> Y^* a complete isometry, where the pairing is <phi, x> = phi(x) - i phi(ix) for phi in Y, x in X. The paper claims that the displayed inequalities ||[x_kl]||_{M_n(X)} <= ||[x_kl]||_{M_n(W)} <= 2||[x_kl]||_{M_n(X)} show that 'Id : W -> X is a real linear isometry and complete contraction with completely bounded inverse', i.e. in particular that at the level n = 1 the two norms coincide exactly.
candidates.suspected_defect: The displayed estimate only gives a factor-2 equivalence, including at n = 1, so it does not by itself establish that Id : W -> X is an isometry; an extra argument (e.g. that Ball(M_1(Y)) is invariant under multiplication by unimodular complex scalars, so that the sup of |phi(x) - i phi(ix)| equals the sup of |phi(x)|) is needed but not given.

candidates.error_location: Theorem 3.1 and its use in the proof of Theorem 3.3 (1)
candidates.exact_quote: Since ℳ^ℝ(Y) = ℳ^ℂ(Y) (this is Theorem 4.5 in [4]), the operator L_i is a real operator space multiplier on (X*)_r. So it is σ(Y, X)-continuous by Theorem 3.1.
candidates.claim_content: Theorem 3.1 is stated as: 'Every operator space left multiplier on a dual operator space is weak* continuous', attributed to [7] (a complex operator space reference). In the proof of Theorem 3.3 (1), X is a REAL operator space, Y = X^† (its real operator space dual) endowed with a complex operator space structure, and u = L_i (multiplication by i) is argued to be a REAL operator space left multiplier of Y_r; Theorem 3.1 is then invoked to conclude that u is sigma(Y,X)-continuous. Also, the identification of the real and complex left multiplier algebras M^R(Y) = M^C(Y) is attributed to [4, Theorem 4.5], whereas in the Closing Remark the same Theorem 4.5 of [4] is cited for the equality of real and complex operator space CENTRALIZERS, Z_R(X) = Z_C(X).
candidates.suspected_defect: Theorem 3.1 is quoted as a complex-operator-space result but applied to a real operator space multiplier on a real dual operator space; the real version is not stated or justified. Additionally, the same cited theorem [4, Theorem 4.5] is used once for multiplier algebras and once for centralizers, so one of the two invocations may be outside the scope of what is proved there. Both would be gaps in the chain leading to the complex structure on X.

candidates.exact_quote:
there is a canonical completely contractive unital homomorphism

\[
I(\mathcal{L}) \cong I(S(X)) \to LM(\mathcal{L}) \subset I(\mathcal{L}),
\]

that compose to the identity, and factors through a *-homomorphism \(\pi : I(S(X)) \to M(\mathcal{L})\).
candidates.claim_content: Setting: X a nonzero (complex) operator space, W = I(X) its injective envelope regarded as a TRO, L = L(W) the TRO linking C*-algebra of W with corners WW^*, W, W^*, W^*W, S(X) the Paulsen system of X, I(S(X)) the injective envelope of S(X), M(L) and LM(L) the multiplier and left multiplier algebras of L. The paper sketches a proof that I(L) ≅ M(L) (the first assertion of [8, Corollary 1.8 (iii)]) by claiming: since L is an ideal in I(S(X)), there are canonical maps I(L) ≅ I(S(X)) -> LM(L) ⊂ I(L) composing to the identity, factoring through a *-homomorphism pi : I(S(X)) -> M(L), which is faithful by the essential property of the injective envelope, hence I(L) ≅ M(L).
candidates.suspected_defect: The sketch is unclear and possibly circular: it uses I(L) ≅ I(S(X)) (which needs justification) as an input to proving I(L) ≅ M(L); it is also not explained why the completely contractive unital map into LM(L) is a *-homomorphism into M(L) (left multipliers need not be two-sided multipliers), nor why the composition is the identity. This sketch is what underpins the 'real case' used in Lemma 3.5, which is in turn used in the proof of Theorem 4.1.

candidates.exact_quote: Conversely, if A has a real predual then it has a complex predual by Theorem 4.1 (or by Remark 2 above), and hence it is a von Neumann algebra by Sakai's theorem
candidates.claim_content: Corollary 4.4 states: a complex C*-algebra A is a complex von Neumann algebra iff it has a real Banach space predual. The proof's converse direction claims that if A has a real predual then it has a complex predual 'by Theorem 4.1 (or by Remark 2 above)'. Remark 2 after Lemma 1.3 states only: 'Any complex Banach space Y with an (isometric) complex predual X clearly has an (isometric) real predual. Indeed (X_r)^† ≅ X^* ≅ Y.' Remark 2 after Theorem 4.1 concerns spaces with (strongly) unique real predual, for which every invertible isometry is weak*-continuous.
candidates.suspected_defect: If 'Remark 2 above' refers to Remark 2 after Lemma 1.3, it gives the opposite implication (complex predual => real predual) and cannot be used here; the alternative justification offered is therefore invalid (the Theorem 4.1 route is fine). If it refers to Remark 2 after Theorem 4.1, the appeal needs the (unstated) fact that A has a strongly unique real predual, which is exactly what is in question.
